hero.title: Your Motivation & Founder Mindset.
hero.intro: Find your reason to begin, turn it into a useful learning habit, and decide how you will respond when evidence challenges your idea. Your deliverable is a Founder Purpose & Learning Plan.

fields.label: What is your honest reason for beginning?
fields.placeholder: I want to use my experience to make event connections more useful.
fields.hint: What would make this journey worthwhile? “I’m exploring” is a valid starting point.

fields.label: Who would you like to help or understand?
fields.placeholder: Visitors who struggle to follow up after events.
fields.hint: Choose people you can realistically learn from, even if the problem is not clear yet.

fields.label: What useful progress would you like in the next four weeks?
fields.placeholder: Understand how five visitors follow up and document unanswered questions.
fields.hint: Choose something within your influence rather than promising sales or investment.

fields.label: What value will guide your decisions?
fields.placeholder: Respect: I will ask permission before recording or sharing information.
fields.hint: Name one value and how it changes your behaviour.

fields.label: What repeatable learning habit will you practise?
fields.placeholder: Every Tuesday at my desk, record one observation and one next question.
fields.hint: Include when, where, action, and output.

fields.label: How will you ask for and use feedback?
fields.placeholder: Ask visitors what they did at their last event; record their words before deciding.
fields.hint: Name a person/group and a question about an actual experience; separate their words from your interpretation.

fields.label: How will you respond when an idea does not help?
fields.placeholder: Pause, ask what was missing, and compare the answer with my assumptions.
fields.hint: Write a practical response that makes space for evidence and a revised next step.

fields.label: What boundary and review point will you set?
fields.placeholder: Two hours a week for four weeks; review on the final Friday and change approach if there is little need.
fields.hint: Include a time/resource limit and when you will decide to continue, change, or pause.

fields.label: What support would help you keep this realistic?
fields.placeholder: Optional: a teammate, mentor, access to people, or a smaller schedule…

fields.label: Where might personal enthusiasm be replacing evidence?
fields.placeholder: I care about… but I have not yet checked…

fields.label: What feedback would make you change your approach?
fields.placeholder: If people tell me or show me… I will reconsider…

fields.label: If your habit does not fit your week, how will you adjust it?
fields.placeholder: I will reduce the action to… and review it on…

questions.prompt: What is a useful purpose statement at this stage?
options: A promise that my business will succeed
A fixed product idea I must defend
A working direction connecting my reason to people I want to help
questions.explanation: A purpose gives direction and can change as you learn. It does not prove demand.

questions.prompt: Which example is a practical learning habit?
options: Every Tuesday, record one observation and one next question
Ignore feedback and work more hours
questions.explanation: A repeatable habit specifies when, action and output, within a realistic schedule.

questions.prompt: When feedback challenges your idea, what helps?
options: Ask about the experience, check assumptions, and decide whether to change
Treat it as a judgment of your worth
Assume one response represents every customer
questions.explanation: Investigate feedback as information; separate an observation from your interpretation and review the approach.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Purpose gives you direction. Learning keeps it honest.

children: Your motivation is your reason for beginning. It may be independence, creating something useful, improving a familiar industry, or exploring a problem you care about. You do not need a dramatic founder story. Start with a reason you can explain in your own words.

A founder mindset means practising useful ways of thinking and acting when the answers are uncertain. It includes curiosity, listening, making manageable commitments, and changing your view when the evidence calls for it.
By the end, you can
Describe why entrepreneurship matters to you.
Connect a personal reason to value for other people.
Turn a useful attitude into a repeatable learning habit.
Respond to feedback with questions rather than instant defence.
Set a practical boundary and a review point.
Motivation: why you begin
“I want more independence” is a valid personal reason. The next question is whose problem you want to understand and how helping them could create value.
A reason is not evidence of customer demand.
Purpose: where you want to contribute
A working purpose links your reason to people: “I want to use my experience in events to help visitors build useful connections.” It can change as you learn.
A purpose is a direction, not a fixed solution.
Habit: what you repeat
Replace “I will be more curious” with “Every Tuesday after work, I will record one observation and one question.” Small, specific actions are easier to review.
Use: when + where + action + output.
Evidence: what you check
If someone does not want your idea, ask about their experience and alternatives. Record what they actually said before drawing a conclusion.
One person's answer is a clue, not the whole market.
An illustrative founder moment

You care about event experiences and suggest a new networking app. A visitor says, “I would not download another app.” A defensive response is to explain more features. A useful response is: “How did you follow up with people at the last event?” Their answer might reveal an existing workaround, a different problem, or little need for your idea.
You can still care about better connections while changing the approach. Keep the purpose flexible enough to learn from people rather than protect a particular product.

blocks.prompt: A potential user says your first idea would not help. Which response helps you learn?

options.label: Explain why they are wrong
options.feedback: Pause and ask about their actual experience. Defending your idea or treating one answer as the whole market prevents useful learning.

options.label: Ask what they do today
options.feedback: Useful response: ask about what they do today, record their experience, and check your assumptions. One response is still only one clue.

options.label: Treat one answer as the whole market
options.feedback: Pause and ask about their actual experience. Defending your idea or treating one answer as the whole market prevents useful learning.

children: Optional practice. Your completion quiz is below.
Persistence needs a review point

Persistence means returning to useful work. It does not mean ignoring evidence, spending beyond your means, or working without rest. Before a small experiment, choose the time and resources you can afford to use. Decide when to review the result and what might lead you to continue, change, or pause.
Confidence can grow through practice.
You can act before feeling fully ready, provided the step is small and responsible. Mindset alone cannot guarantee a viable business, funding, or commercial success.
Three terms to keep clear
Feedback:
what someone tells you about their experience or reaction.
Interpretation:
what you think that feedback means.
Learning habit:
a repeated action that helps you gather information and reflect.
You can record “I’m still exploring” as your purpose today. Choose a reachable group, one learning habit, and a review point rather than inventing certainty.
Write a working purpose and a small plan you can review. You are setting a direction, not promising a business outcome. Use short concrete answers; avoid sensitive personal information.

sections.label: 05 / CHALLENGE
sections.heading: Challenge the plan, not your worth.

children: Use these questions to check whether your purpose and habits will help you learn.
More questions to discuss
Does your purpose describe a benefit to someone else, or only a product you want to build?
Are you setting a goal you can influence?
Do you have a clear point to review time, cost and evidence?
Can you pause a weak approach without treating it as a personal failure?
Answer all three. You can retry; all three correct are required for local completion.
